## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

A three-juan commentary on *[DZ 10 Gāoshàng Yùhuáng běnxíng jíjīng](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR5/KR5a/KR5a0010)* formally attributed to Zhāng Liáng 張良 — the Western-Hàn strategist of Liú Bāng 劉邦 who died 187 BCE — in his posthumous deified office as *Tiānshū shàngxiàng* 天樞上相, "Supreme Minister of the Celestial Pivot [= Polaris / Dǒuxīng 斗星]." The attribution is transparently spurious, and the text is of late Sòng or Yuán provenance, but the commentarial fiction is carried through with scrupulous consistency: each juan opens with a line-heading attribution 天樞上相(臣)張良校正 ("collated by the Supreme Minister of the Celestial Pivot, [your servant] Zhāng Liáng"), and Zhāng's interlinear comments — prefaced by "(臣)良曰" ("your servant Liáng says") or "(臣)謹言" — expound each passage of the parent scripture in the register of a Hàn court-memorial addressed upward to the Jade Emperor.

The *běnwén* portion of the commentary exactly reproduces DZ 10 and is interleaved with Zhāng Liáng's memorial-style explications. The text is preceded by a group of spurious celestial-bureaucratic documents (the *Sāntiān ménxià jiàojīng zhàowén* 三天門下校經詔文, "Edict from the Chancellery of the Three Heavens for the Collation of the Scripture"), purportedly transmitted by two otherwise-unknown "saints" Lín Shàohuá 林少華 (receiving) and Cāng Rújiā 蒼汝嘉 (delivering), appointing Zhāng to the collation task. Following the three juan is an appendix, *Sòngjīng gǎnyìng* 誦經感應 ("Efficacy-Tales of Scripture Recitation"), in four folios, comprising seven miraculous-response anecdotes set in the Súi (581–618) and Táng (618–907) — anecdotes drawn (anonymously) from the wider *lìngyàn* 靈驗 ("numinous-efficacy") literature.

**Abstract**

This text is pseudepigraphic: its attribution to Zhāng Liáng in his posthumous celestial office has no basis in the historical transmission of Daoist scripture. Zhāng Liáng (d. 187 BCE) was the Western-Hàn strategist of the Gāozǔ 高祖 court whose historical-biographical tradition is recorded in *Shǐjì* 史記 55 and *Hànshū* 漢書 40; his deification as a celestial minister belongs to the later Daoist pantheon-organising imagination and is visible by the Tang in connection with the *Tiānshū* 天樞 (Polaris) cult but is fully deployed here only in the service of authorising a commentary on a scripture that itself was not in circulation before the thirteenth century. The text's own dating is entirely dependent on the parent scripture [DZ 10](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR5/KR5a/KR5a0010), which is a late-Southern-Sòng or early-Yuán Qīngwēi-school 清微 production first documented in 1240 at Hángzhōu. Kristofer Schipper, in Schipper & Verellen eds., *The Taoist Canon* (2004) 2:1097, §3.B.7, remarks that "the text yields no clues as to the date of its compilation" and that the spurious delivering-saints Lín Shàohuá and Cāng Rújiā are "unknown." The frontmatter here brackets the composition notBefore 1240 (the earliest documented circulation of the parent scripture) / notAfter 1445 (the printing of the *Zhèngtǒng Dàozàng*), with dynasty given as 南宋—明初.

Schipper notes further that it is "difficult to say whether [the text's] placement [in the Daozang] is the result of an oversight by the compilers or whether this commentary was equally considered to be a *běnwén*" — i.e., whether the Ming editors treated the Zhāng Liáng commentary as part of the "fundamental scripture" proper. The Dàozàng jíyào 道藏輯要 handles the question decisively by collating DZ 10 and DZ 11 together under a single JY088 entry.

The appendix *Sòngjīng gǎnyìng* carries seven miraculous-response anecdotes, all set in Súi and Táng; their sources are not given. Comparable *gǎnyìng* appendices are standard in late-Sòng and Yuán Qīngwēi-school scripture-editions and function as marketing material for recitation.

**On persons:** the catalog meta attributes the text to Zhāng Liáng; frontmatter accordingly carries the wikilink `"[張良](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BC%B5%E8%89%AF) (attributed 校正, as 天樞上相)"`. Lín Shàohuá and Cāng Rújiā appear only in the pseudo-imperial apparatus of the text and are Daoist celestial-office fictions; they are mentioned in prose but not wikilinked.
